content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new speech pre-training algorithm that incorporates unpaired text data. In order to align the speech and text representation, the algorithm introduces a small set of paired text-speech data to learn the alignment. The paper shows the competitive performance of the proposed algorithm in a number of speech-processing downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths:

1. The techniques proposed in this paper are plausible, and the resulting performance is competitive.
2. The findings in this paper that incorporating text into speech training can benefit speech downstream tasks can shed some light on the future directions of speech pretraining models.

### Weaknesses:

1. The clarity of the paper can be greatly improved. The paper introduces a lot of terms and notations without first highlighting how these different modules are connected. Sometimes the symbols are misused. More specifically,

- In equation (1), both the speech and text discrete units are represented as $Z$ without any differentiation. In the latter text, the $Z$ symbol is used without explaining whether it is from text or from speech. For instance, under section 3.2 'Shared Transformer' paragraph, '$U$, which is derived from the tokenized units $Z$ by an embedding layer...' Does this $Z$ come from both text and speech? Or is it just from text? In figure 2, it looks like the $U$ is only derived from the $Z$ at the text end, but it is impossible to disambiguate from reading the text without referring to Figure 2.

- Under section 3.2 'Shared Transformer', 'We randomly select some positions ... and replace the lower representation $h^{L/2}$ with the corresponding unit embedding $u_i$, where the unit are extracted from the input speech sample'. Doesn't $U$ come from the text input? Figure 2 seems to suggest that $U$ only comes from text. Also, and the start of section 3.2 'Shared Transformer', it is clearly mentioned that 'speech representation $H^{L/2}$ and **textual representation** $U$'. So it is never mentioned elsewhere that $U$ can be derived from the speech input, so this is very confusing to me. Also, in figure 2, the input to the swapping mechanism is $Z$, not $U$, so clearly a contradiction with the text description.

- In and below equation 1, the discrete unit sequence is represented as $Z$. However, above equation 4, it is represented as $U$ instead.

- There are also quite a few typos and minor mistakes. I would suggest the authors perform a thorough check.

2. The experiment results do not fully support the claims made in the paper. In fact, and the paper mentioned, there are already some existing pre-training algorithms that involve text, The paper claims that SpeechLM is superior to the existing work in that it is able the align the hidden space of speech and text. However, very few evaluations include other speech-text joint training algorithms as baselines. For example, the ASR task involves mostly speech-only pre-training algorithms. So the experiment can only establish that incorporating text and benefit speech pre-training, which is already proven. It has not been established that SpeechLM can incorporate text information better than the other algorithms. It would be very helpful if the authors can include more joint training baselines.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Clarity
The clarity is a major weakness of the paper. See 'Strength and Weakness' for more details.

### Quality
This is solid work with careful engineering designs, but the empirical evaluation can be improved.

### Novelty
The novelty over the existing work is a bit incremental. Speech and text joint training has been previously explored. The major novelty in this paper is that SpeechLM introduces an alignment mechanism to unify speech and text representation. The technical contribution is good, but not great.

### Reproducibility
The paper contains sufficient implementation details.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper develops a competitive speech-text joint-training algorithm and plausible technical innovations. However, the clarity of the presentation can be improved and the experiments should include more joint training baselines. The innovation is not strong enough for ICLR.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2274 by Reviewer EUSA

content.title: Response to reviewer EUSA
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and suggestions. We have improved our paper according to your suggestions in our new version.

> **Q1: The confusion about the $Z$ and $U$ from speech and text.**

A1: Thanks for pointing out it. It might be indeed a misleading description in this paper. 

$u$ in our paper means the unit embeddings of the discrete units $z$ (and the sequence are denoted as $U$ and $Z$), i.e. $u=Embedding(z)$. As we use unified tokenizers, discrete units can be tokenized from either text or speech. So, the Embedding layer can not only process the units from the text but also process the units from the speech. As in the U-CTC task, the input units $Z$ are from text, so the unit embeddings $U$ are just from text. As in the “Random Swapping” mechanism, the unpaired speech and its tokenized units $Z$ (here $Z$ are from speech) are synchronized frame by frame. So we first process some of these units $z_i$ into the unit embeddings $u_i$, and then use such $u_i$ to replace the speech hidden states. Here $z_i$ and $u_i$ are from speech and $i$ is one of the selected time positions.

> "Also, in figure 2, the input to the swapping mechanism is Z, not U"

As explained, the input to the swapping is the unit embeddings $u_i$ of the units $z_i$ derived from speech, we omitted the Embedding layer in Fig 1, which has been added in the revised version.

> "In and below equation 1, the discrete unit sequence is represented as $Z$. However, above equation 4, it is represented as $U$ instead."

In equation 4, the condition is represented as $U^L$, not $U$, which means the $L$-th transformer layer’s output.

Overall, to overcome this confusion, we have made a clearer description in Section 3 and have modified Figure 1, mainly adding subscripts to the symbols, e.g. $z$ to $z_S$ and $z_T$, $u$ to $u_S$ and $u_T$.

> **The experiment results lack the comparison with previous speech-text joint training baselines.**

A2: The main reason we did not list some speech-text joint training baselines is that the model and data size varies largely among previous speech-text joint training works, making it hard for a fair comparison. The most related works are SLAM and MAESTRO, whose experimental settings need too many computation resources to follow (e.g. X-Large model), which are beyond our resource limitation.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2274 by Reviewer VrdX

content.title: Response to reviewer VrdX
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful suggestions and comments. Thanks for your guidance about the “state-of-the-art” words used in the paper, where the performance gains are constrained by the model and data size. We would try to emphasize these constraints and make a clearer description of the results.

> **Q1: It's unclear how scalable the phoneme tokenizer is when aiming language expansion. Lexicon is a strong supervise signal.**

A1: Thanks for this constructive comment. We agree that phonemes are highly language-specific and human designed, which might be less transferable across languages. So, in this paper, we also provided hidden-unit based tokenizers, which is alternative to phoneme-base tokenizers and doesn’t need a lexicon. Moreover, we want to emphasize that our main idea is to propose to use unified tokenizers for both speech and text and show both phoneme and hidden units work. As for the further strengths or limitations of each tokenizer, we would like to leave it for future investigation.

> **Q2: It's unclear if it is helpful for ASR. The best reported results are much worse than previous SoTA (not comparable in model size)**

A2: Our proposed methods are beneficial for ASR tasks. 

In this paper, we evaluate our model under two most commonly used settings in previous works (Wav2vec, HuBERT, WavLM, et al): 
- The **Base** setting where the model is pre-trained on 960h and fine-tuned on 100h with a 100M model. In the Base setting, our ASR results outperform the previous works including HuBERT, wavLM, data2vec, et al with significant improvement. At the same time, we don't use more paired data since the paired data for training our tokenizers are included in the fine-tuning data.
- The **Large** setting where the model is pre-trained on 60kh and fine-tuned on 960h with a 300M model. In the large setting, we achieve competitive results compared to previous works (e.g., we achieve 1.8/3.2 WER compared with 1.9/3.3 of HuBERT with a language model, and our 1.9/3.6 WER compared with 2.1/4.2 of HuBERT without language model).

> "If look at low resource, ..., why not just finetune on 100h, and compare with Hubert, which is 2.1/3.9."

We didn’t evaluate the model in the 60kh->100h setting, since our tokenizer is trained on 960h paired data for Large models. We think it makes no sense to fine-tune on a smaller paired dataset (since we have already used 960h paired data).
Based on your comments, we think that maybe the organization of Table 1 confuses you. We will reorganize it to make it clearer (by adding specific data conditions). What’s more, we agree that the performance gains are less significant in the Large setting.

> **Q3: No comparison with MAESTRO**

A3: We did not compare it with MAESTRO model, since it is unfair at least in three aspects as follows.  
First, the smallest model reported in Maestro is X-Large model (600M), which is beyond our computation limitations (Base and Large for our setting). Second, MAESTRO uses much more labeled data (the whole SpeechStrew, about 5kh paired data) than ours during the pre-training. Third, MAESTRO uses RNN-T framework, but our model employs CTC framework without a decoder, which is to align with many other models like wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT.

> **Q4: Section 4.4 looks like a fairer comparison. Can the author add how text data affect those results?**

A4: Thanks for this comment. We think there are two reasons. First, because SpeechLM uses the shared discrete representation for both speech and text, textual data can boost the quality of speech representation learning, which is beneficial for downstream tasks. Second, speech-to-text translation is more difficult than text-to-text translation since the former must model both the cross-modal conversion and cross-lingual conversion. SpeechLM employs phoneme units and hidden units as the bridge between speech and text. Hence, in speech translation tasks, SpeechLM can effectively convert the source audio into a well-defined intermediate representation, which will greatly reduce the burden of cross-modal conversion of speech-to-text translation and improve the translation quality. We will add this discussion in our new version.

content.title: Response to reviewer LP8q
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments, here we would like to respond to your concerns about the paper.

> **Q1: The innovation of this work on top of the prior works SLAM and MAESTRO**

A1: The biggest innovation of our work is that we proposed two alternative tokenizers which can convert unlabeled speech and text into the **shared discrete space** and eliminate the influence of modal difference on joint modeling. Specifically, the proposed model differs from SLAM and MAESTRO in 3 major aspects:
- **The proposed SpeechLM utilizes a unified discrete space for speech and text modalities, which significantly unifies and simplifies the model pre-training.** In SLAM, the authors individually design w2v-bert loss (based on contrastive loss) for unsupervised speech, BERT loss for unpaired text, and TLM/STM losses for the paired data. Though these losses are also based on MLM and CTC, they use uncorrelated input/target data for each task. This might lead the model to use individual capacities to handle each modality and thus might miss the goal of alignment. The speech and the text in SLAM are not guaranteed to lie in the same space, leading to transfer interference and capacity dilution issues [1]. 
Similar to SLAM, MAESTRO also designs multiple different tasks for unpaired speech, unpaired text, and paired data, i.e. w2v-bert loss for speech, text-to-text RNNT loss for text, MSE loss for paired data.
Unlike them, our model uses unified discrete units which participate in both the speech task and the text task. That could simplify the model pre-training with only two prediction tasks (speech-to-unit MLM and unit-to-text CTC).

- **By leveraging unified units, it is expected to align the speech and text during pre-training with the whole unpaired data, while SLAM and MAESTRO only rely on paired data for the alignment.** SLAM and MEASTRO used TLM/SLM loss or modality MSE loss to achieve the alignment of speech and text. While such losses can only be performed on speech-text paired data that are jointly optimized during pre-training. Different from them, we use offline tokenizers to convert speech/text to a unified modality, making it more natural to align the two modalities, and the whole unpaired speech/text data could convey this alignment information.

- **We consider the "Random Swapping" is not just a small trick but a necessary complementation to our main idea of using unified units in this paper.** This necessity is confirmed during our experiments (Table. 4). The "Random Swapping" plays the role of shuffling two modalities, making the model treats the lower representations of speech and units the same way. In the revised paper, we would pay more attention to explain the "Random Swapping" mechanism.

> **Q2: ASR results from SLAM are missing in Table 1**

A2: Because SLAM only has the setting of X-Large model, which is significantly larger than our setting (Base and Large), so we did not list the ASR results of SLAM in Table 1 for a fair comparison.

Table 1 lists the results in Base setting (960h pre-train, 100h fine-tune with 100M model) and Large setting (60k pre-train, 960 fine-tune with 300M model). Unfortunately, the smallest model reported by SLAM is X-Large model (600M). Due to the performance gap with different model sizes (see Table III in the HuBERT paper[2] for an investigation of model size), and pre-training a X-Large model is beyond our computation limitations, we didn’t report the result of X-Large models.

> **Q3: Questions about the description on "Random Swapping Mechanism"**

We are sorry for the unclear description of this part.  $u$ in our paper means the unit embeddings of the discrete units $z$, i.e., $u=Embedding(z)$. As we use the unified tokenizers, units can be tokenized from either text or speech. So, the **Embedding** layer can not only process the units from the text but also process the units from the speech. As in the “Random Swapping” section, the unpaired speech and its tokenized units $z$ are synchronized frame by frame. So, we can process some of these units $z_i$ into unit embeddings $u_i$, and then use such $u_i$ to replace the speech hidden states. In this way, we can shuffle two modalities into one sequence and let the model treat them equally. As you suggested, we have emphasized the “Random Swapping” more in the paper and have given a more specified description of it.

Also, to reduce confusion about the discrete units and their embedding, we have made modifications to the paper, mainly adding subscripts to the symbols, e.g. $z$ to $z_S$ and $z_T$, $u$ to $u_S$ and $u_T$.

[1] Ankur Bapna, et al, A unified encoder for speech and language modeling via speech-text joint pre-training. arXiv preprint arXiv:2110.10329, 2021.

[2] Wei-Ning Hsu, et al. Hubert: Self-supervised speech representation learning by masked prediction of hidden units. IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, 29:3451–3460, 2021.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes pre-training jointly on speech and text data by using tokenizers for text and speech and propose an architecture that maps representations from text and speech into a common space. The paper shows significant improvements on the standard speech tasks, such as ASR, SUPERB benchmark and speech translation.

The tokenizers in this paper are trained using a) 100h (or more) of paired speech/text data, b) word/phone lexicon, c) pre-trained hubert models, d) a modified model that is trained to map from phonemized text into hidden units and they are the key to obtain good performance with this setup.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Excellent performance across various tasks
- Relatively straight forward explanation of the setup
- Novel approach to mapping speech and text units into the same representational space, supported by analysis

Weaknesses:
- Reliance on tokenizers that require paired data, lexicon and additional pre-trained models setup an unfair comparison to other models (exemplified by Figure 1 and the abstract) which do not use extra resources. While it's great to compare to a bunch of baselines, it might be good to make it very clear that the proposed model uses additional resources and (due to the tokenizer pipeline) is significantly more expensive to train end to end.
- What is the minimum amount of paired data required to build well-performing tokenizers? Might be good to have an ablation on this topic.

Other:
- have you tried combining the two tokenizers in a single model?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is pretty straight forward to follow, and the approach seems to be novel and achieves impressive results. The authors promise to release the model and the code which will allow others to reproduce this work.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper proposes a novel method to combine text and speech data for pre-training, by utilizing a pipeline of tokenizers that requires additional paired data and/or other pre-trained models. The results are impressive and the approach is novel and, I believe, is interesting to the community. One suggestions for the authors is to consider being more explicit about the additional resources required to build such a model in their comparisons to existing methods.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2274 by Reviewer q8bU

content.title: Response to Reviewer q8bU
content.comment:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful comments and questions, we would like to give detailed responses to your comments below.

**Q1: Reliance on tokenizers that require paired data, lexicon and additional pre-trained models setup an unfair comparison to other models.**

A1: It is true that our proposed model uses additional resources for training tokenizers, and we will make it clearer in our new version according to your suggestion. Here, we want to emphasize that the most important part of the extra resource (i.e., the paired data) does not exceed the scope of the fine-tuning data in the ASR task. It means that we use the same amount of paired data as in other previous works if we consider the whole pre-training/finetuning pipeline.

Moreover, additional tokenizer models are also used in many baselines, such as HuBERT and WavLM. We have tried to specify the difference in data among different methods in Table 1. As you suggested, we will give a specified description of other tokenizer-related resources in our paper to make a clearer comparison with other models.

**Q2: The minimum amount of paired data required to build well-performing tokenizers?**

A2: Thanks for your good question and suggestion. Currently, we use paired data which is the same as fine-tuning set as our training data of tokenizers. It is a good suggestion to explore what is the minimum amount of paired data for the tokenizers.

**Q3: Combining the two tokenizers in a single model?**

A3: That is a very constructive suggestion. In this paper, we mainly aim to bridge speech and text with a unified discrete representation, and we provide two different options about the tokenizers, both of which can work well. We also did a preliminary exploration of combining the two tokenizers, whose results are not listed in the current paper. We simply used hidden units might as the target labels of Speech Transformer and used phoneme units as the target labels of Shared Transformer. It only achieved comparable results with SpeechLM-P models (2.6/5.7 vs. 2.5/5.7). How to combine the two tokenized units is an interesting following work, we would like to further investigate it in the future.
